title: L'Allegro: title, date and companion poem
short: Italian for 'the cheerful man'; the first of a matched pair with Il Penseroso, printed together in Milton's Poems (1645).
body: The Italian title names a temperament rather than a person: 'the cheerful, merry man'. The poem was printed with its companion Il Penseroso ('the pensive man') in Poems of Mr. John Milton (dated 1645, issued early 1646). The date of composition is uncertain; neither poem is in the Trinity Manuscript, and most editors place them in the early 1630s, around or just after Milton left Cambridge (1629-32). E. M. W. Tillyard linked the pair to Milton's academic exercise Prolusion I, on whether day or night is more excellent, and the poems do follow one ideal day and one ideal night. Each opens by banishing the other's presiding spirit and closes by choosing to live with its own goddess. Samuel Johnson thought every reader reads them with pleasure and stressed that each mind selects the objects that suit it.

title: The exorcism prelude and its metre
short: Ten lines alternating short (six-syllable) and long (ten-syllable) lines, before the poem settles into octosyllabic couplets at l. 11.
body: The opening exorcism is formally set off from the rest. Its ten lines alternate iambic trimeter and pentameter on an interlaced rhyme scheme (abbacddeec), giving a heavy, deliberately over-emphatic effect suited to a mock-solemn banishing. At l. 11 ('But com thou Goddes fair and free') the poem shifts to the light four-stress couplets, often with the first syllable dropped (seven syllables), that carry the rest of it. Il Penseroso begins with exactly the same ten-line pattern, so the two openings mirror each other. Editors note the parody of the classical hymn of banishment (the formula 'procul este, profani'), and the genealogy Milton gives Melancholy here, from Cerberus and Night, is his own invention, a grotesque counterpart to the noble parentage she receives in Il Penseroso.

title: Cerberus
short: The three-headed watchdog of the underworld, here made Melancholy's father by a mock genealogy of Milton's own devising.
body: Cerberus guards the gate of Hades (Hesiod, Theogony 310-12, makes him a child of Typhon and Echidna; Virgil, Aeneid 6.417-25). No classical source makes him the father of Melancholy: Milton coins the pedigree to make the gloomy, bile-driven melancholy banished here as monstrous as possible. Pairing him with 'blackest midnight' recalls Hesiod's Night, who bears a brood of evils (Theogony 211-25). The point is that this is the diseased melancholy of the physicians, black bile, not the contemplative melancholy that Il Penseroso will honour with a nobler descent from Saturn and Vesta.

title: Cimmerian desert
short: The land of perpetual darkness at the edge of the world, visited by Odysseus on his way to the dead.
body: In Odyssey 11.14-19 the Cimmerians live at the edge of Ocean, shrouded in mist and cloud, where the sun never shines. 'Cimmerian' became a byword for total darkness. Milton sends Melancholy to the bleakest place classical geography could supply; 'desert' means a deserted, uninhabited region rather than a sandy waste. Ebon shades and low-browed rocks (l. 8) complete a scene that is half underworld, half Gothic picture.

title: ycleap'd Euphrosyne
short: 'Called' (archaic, Spenserian) Euphrosyne, Greek 'mirth, good cheer', one of the three Graces.
body: 'Ycleap'd' is the old past participle of 'clepe', to call or name, with the Middle English y- prefix; Milton borrows it from the Spenserian archaic vocabulary. Euphrosyne (Greek euphrosyne, 'merriment, good cheer') is one of the three Graces with Aglaia and Thalia; Hesiod makes them daughters of Zeus and Eurynome (Theogony 907-9). The contrast 'In Heav'n ... And by men' imitates the Homeric habit of giving a thing its name among the gods and its name among mortals.

title: Venus and Bacchus as parents
short: Mirth is first given Venus and Bacchus as parents, a genealogy found only in late commentary (Servius on the Aeneid).
body: The Graces are usually daughters of Zeus; the version making them children of Venus and Bacchus (love and wine) survives in Servius's commentary on the Aeneid (on 1.720), as Osgood noted. Ivy was sacred to Bacchus. Milton then sets this parentage aside in favour of what 'Sager' poets sing (l. 17), perhaps because love and wine suggest a grosser pleasure than the 'unreproved' mirth the poem wants (l. 40).

title: Zephyr and Aurora
short: The 'sager' alternative genealogy: Mirth born of the west wind and the dawn on a May morning, apparently Milton's own invention.
body: No classical source makes Zephyr (the mild west wind of spring) the lover of Aurora (the dawn); in Hesiod the dawn is the mother of the winds, and her consort is Tithonus. Osgood therefore treats the pairing as Milton's departure from tradition. Its fitness is clear: the cheerful man's day begins at dawn, in fresh spring air, and the scene of 'a Maying', violets and dew-washed roses gives Mirth an innocent, outdoor, English birth instead of a Bacchic one. 'Bucksom' (l. 24) here means lively and yielding, from Middle English buhsum, 'obliging, pliant'; 'debonair' means gracious and courteous (Old French de bon aire).

title: the light fantastick toe
short: Dance lightly and whimsically; one of the most quoted (and later cliched) phrases in the poem.
body: 'Trip it' means dance with quick light steps; 'fantastick' means fanciful, capricious, following the play of fancy. The phrase became proverbial in the eighteenth century, when the two poems were endlessly imitated, and it is now chiefly used humorously. Its rhythm enacts the dance: the line's quick unstressed syllables carry the feet forward. The address 'ye' (l. 33) includes Mirth's whole train, not only the goddess, so the poem pictures a group dance led by Mirth with Liberty at her right hand.

title: The Mountain Nymph, sweet Liberty
short: Liberty pictured as an oread, a mountain nymph; Mirth and freedom go together.
body: Mountain peoples were traditionally thought hardy and free, and editors compare the mountain nymphs (oreads) of classical pastoral. The line has often been read with hindsight in the light of Milton's later republican writings, but in the poem liberty chiefly means freedom from care and constraint, the condition of 'unreproved pleasures free' (l. 40). 'Unreproved' means blameless, beyond reproach: Milton stresses that this mirth is innocent.

anchor: at my window bid good morrow
title: Who comes to the window?
short: A famous syntactic puzzle: is it the lark or the speaker who comes 'in spight of sorrow' to the window?
body: Grammatically, 'Then to com' (l. 45) may continue 'To hear the Lark' (l. 41), so that the cheerful man himself rises and comes to his window to say good morning through the sweet-briar and vine. Alternatively the lark is the subject, coming to the window to bid the sleeper good morrow, which is ornithologically odd since larks do not visit windows. Some readers have even made the dawn the subject. Editors have not agreed, and the Variorum sets out the long history of the debate. The ambiguity keeps the waking man and the waking world blended. 'Eglantine' is itself another name for the sweet-briar, so some editors have wondered whether Milton meant honeysuckle by 'twisted Eglantine'.

title: the Cock and his Dames
short: The rooster struts in front of his hens; he 'scatters the rear' of departing night like a soldier routing a retreating army.
body: 'Scatters the rear of darknes thin' is a military metaphor: the cock's crowing chases off the rear-guard of night's retreating forces. 'His Dames' are his hens, mock-chivalric. The rustic scene is generalised rather than particular, and Johnson's summary of the poem singles it out: the cheerful man 'sees the cock strut'. At l. 114 the cock reappears ringing his 'Mattin' at the end of the night.

title: the Sun's state
short: The rising sun as a monarch beginning a royal procession, with clouds dressed as his liveried servants.
body: 'State' means royal pomp or a stately progress (OED). The 'Eastern gate' is the classical gate of the dawn. The clouds wear 'thousand Liveries', the uniforms of a great lord's retinue, and are 'dight' (dressed, adorned, an archaic past participle). 'Not unseen' (l. 57) is pointed: the cheerful man walks in company and in daylight, whereas the pensive man walks 'unseen' (Il Penseroso 65).

title: every Shepherd tells his tale
short: Either 'counts his flock' (tale = tally) or 'tells a story', perhaps a love tale; editors have disagreed since the eighteenth century.
body: 'Tell' can mean 'count' and 'tale' can mean 'number, tally' (compare 'teller' of votes and the phrase 'the tale of bricks' in Exodus 5:8, KJV). Warton argued that the shepherd counts his sheep at dawn as they leave the fold, a practical rural task in a list of workers (ploughman, milkmaid, mower). Others read a story or love tale told under the hawthorn, a pastoral commonplace. Both senses were current, and the line may hold both.

title: Lantskip
short: 'Landscape', from Dutch landschap; then a painter's word for a view seen as a picture.
body: The word entered English around 1600 from Dutch painting vocabulary, so 'Lantskip' keeps its sense of a composed scene; the eye 'measures' it as a painter would. The following list ('Russet Lawns, and Fallows Gray', mountains, meadows, brooks, towers) is arranged like a picture with foreground and distance. 'Lawns' are open grassy spaces, 'fallows' ploughed land left unsown, and 'pide' (l. 75) means variegated.

title: Cynosure
short: The Little Bear or Pole Star, by which sailors steered; hence the centre of everyone's gaze.
body: Greek kynosoura, 'dog's tail', named the constellation Ursa Minor, whose tail holds the Pole Star; mariners looked to it to steer, so it became a figure for whatever draws all eyes. Milton's line is an early figurative use in English, of the kind that lies behind the modern sense of 'centre of attention'. The beauty 'bosom'd high in tufted Trees' is the lady of a castle seen from afar, a romance motif. Compare Comus 341-42, where Milton again uses the 'Cynosure' as a guiding star.

title: Corydon, Thyrsis, Phillis, Thestylis
short: Stock names from Theocritus and Virgil's Eclogues, here given to English farm labourers.
body: Corydon and Thyrsis compete in song in Virgil's Eclogue 7; Phyllis appears in Eclogues 3 and 7; Thestylis prepares a meal of herbs for the reapers in Eclogue 2.10-11. Milton transfers the classical names to an English cottage with its 'savory dinner' of herbs and 'Country Messes' (dishes). The effect is gently literary: the real countryside is seen through Virgilian pastoral. 'Neat-handed' means deft.

title: rebecks; Sunshine Holyday
short: A rebeck is a small medieval fiddle; the scene is a village festival with bells, dance and ale.
body: The rebec, a bowed instrument of two or three strings, was by Milton's time a rustic fiddle. 'Up-land Hamlets' are hill villages; 'secure' (l. 91) means carefree (Latin securus, 'without care'), not 'safe'. 'Chequer'd shade' is the dappled shadow of leaves. Village wakes, maypoles and Sunday sports were politically sensitive in the 1630s: Charles I's reissued Book of Sports (1633) defended them against Puritan objections, and some critics read the passage against that controversy, though Milton presents it without polemic.

title: Faery Mab and the junkets
short: Fireside tales of the fairy queen Mab, who eats the cream dishes left out, and of the will-o'-the-wisp.
body: Queen Mab, the fairies' midwife, is described by Mercutio in Romeo and Juliet 1.4, and Jonson brought her on stage in his Entertainment at Althorp (1603). 'Junkets' are sweet dishes of cream or curds. 'She was pincht, and pull'd' refers to the fairies' punishment of slovenly maids. 'Friars Lanthorn' is the ignis fatuus or will-o'-the-wisp, the marsh light that led night travellers astray (also 'Friar Rush's lantern'). The storytellers alternate (she ... he), a realistic touch of village gossip.

title: The drudging Goblin / Lubbar Fend
short: Robin Goodfellow or Hobgoblin, the household spirit who does a night's threshing for a bowl of cream, then sprawls by the fire.
body: Folklore told of a hairy household spirit who did farm work overnight in return for a bowl of cream set out for him; Reginald Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) mentions the bowl of milk left for Robin Goodfellow, and Puck boasts of the same character in A Midsummer Night's Dream 2.1. A 'lubber fiend' is a clumsy, loutish demon (lubber = lout). 'Shadowy Flale' is the ghostly flail; 'Crop-full' means with full belly; 'Mattin' is matins, the first canonical hour, here the cock's crow before dawn.

title: Ladies whose bright eies Rain influence
short: The ladies' eyes act like stars, raining down astrological 'influence' on the knights at the tournament.
body: The scene shifts to 'Towred Cities' and courtly romance: knights in 'weeds of Peace' (court dress, not armour) hold 'triumphs' (festivities, pageants, tournaments). 'Influence' is the astrological fluid believed to stream from the stars and shape human affairs (Latin influere, 'to flow in'); the ladies' eyes are stars that judge the prize of wit or arms. The image is Petrarchan and Spenserian, and fits the court masques and tilts of Jacobean and Caroline England.

title: Hymen in saffron robe
short: The god of marriage, traditionally dressed in saffron yellow and carrying a torch, as in Ovid and in court masques.
body: Ovid opens Metamorphoses 10 with Hymen arriving 'croceo velatus amictu', veiled in a saffron cloak, for the ill-fated wedding of Orpheus and Eurydice, so his appearance here quietly anticipates the Orpheus ending of the poem. Hymen with his taper (wedding torch) was a stock figure of Jonson's wedding masques such as Hymenaei (1606). 'Mask' is masque, and 'antique Pageantry' may mean both 'ancient' and 'antic' (grotesque) display, the spelling not distinguishing them.

title: Jonson's learned sock and Shakespeare's wood-notes
short: Comedy (the 'sock' of the comic actor) by the learned Jonson, set against Shakespeare's untaught natural genius.
body: The soccus was the low slipper worn by actors in Roman comedy, as the cothurnus or buskin was the tragic boot (compare Il Penseroso 102). Jonson's comedies are 'learned' because they follow classical models; Shakespeare is 'fancies childe' warbling 'native Wood-notes wilde', like a songbird untaught by art. This contrast of art and nature became a critical commonplace, already present in Jonson's own folio poem (1623) with its 'small Latine, and lesse Greeke'. Milton's sonnet 'On Shakespear' (printed 1632) praises him for 'easie numbers' that flow without labour. Many later readers have found the 'wood-notes' line condescending.

title: soft Lydian Aires
short: Music in the Lydian mode, which Plato banned as soft and convivial; Milton welcomes it, wed to great poetry.
body: Greek theory linked each musical mode to an emotional effect. In Republic 3.398e-399a Plato's Socrates excludes the Lydian modes from his ideal city as slack and suited to drinking. Milton's cheerful man asks for exactly that softness 'against eating Cares', but makes it respectable by marrying the music 'to immortal verse', a union Milton returns to in 'At a Solemn Music'. The long sentence that follows, with its 'winding bout' (turn, circuit) and 'lincked sweetnes long drawn out', enacts the melisma it describes. 'Wanton heed, and giddy cunning' are deliberate oxymorons: a careful carelessness, a whirling skill.

title: Orpheus and Eurydice
short: Orpheus's song won Eurydice back from Pluto, but he lost her by looking back; this music would have freed her completely.
body: Orpheus charmed Pluto with his lyre and was allowed to lead his dead wife Eurydice out of Hades on condition he did not look back; he looked, and lost her (Virgil, Georgics 4.453-527; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.1-85). Milton imagines Orpheus lifting his head from the flowers of Elysium to hear music that would have won her outright. Orpheus recurs in Il Penseroso 105-8 and, more darkly, in 'Lycidas' 58-63, where he is torn apart.

anchor: These delights, if thou canst give
title: Closing couplet and Marlowe
short: The poem ends by echoing Marlowe's 'Passionate Shepherd': if Mirth gives these delights, he will live with her.
body: Marlowe's lyric ends: 'If these delights thy mind may move, / Then live with me, and be my love.' Milton turns the shepherd's invitation around: the poet accepts the goddess's offer conditionally. The conditional 'if' leaves the choice open, and Il Penseroso ends with the same formula addressed to Melancholy ('And I with thee will choose to live'). Critics have long debated whether the pair presents a progression from mirth to the higher contemplative life, or two equally valid modes; others see two equally valid modes of life.
